title: Grade XI Physics – Unit 1: Physical Quantities and Measurements
limitations: Pilot currently contains 47 source-reviewed conceptual MCQs: 24 from the initial pilot and 23 new text-safe selections from a 275-question SLO source bank.
Of the 275 source MCQs, 200 contain Word equation objects. These are not yet imported; conversion and visual validation are required.
Stimulus question sets and text-only questions that require a preceding shared passage are not included.
Does not yet cover every summative theory SLO, application-level calculations, or the official FBISE full-paper blueprint.
All published SLO mappings are supporting classifications requiring detailed teacher review; boardEligible=false.
Printed textbook page numbers are still pending verification.
Source author Word answer keys have been preserved for the additional 23 items, without changing their wording.
Do not present this bank as an exact FBISE examination or an exhaustive Unit 1 assessment.

questions.stem: An estimation of a physical quantity is best described as:

options.text: a rough educated value based on experience and physical reasoning
a value having no physical unit

questions.explanation: Estimation is a reasoned approximate value based on experience and physical reasoning.

questions.stem: Which statement about estimation is correct?

options.text: It must always equal the exact measured value.
It involves reasonable assumptions and physical reasoning.
It does not require any knowledge of the situation.
It is useful only for microscopic quantities.

questions.explanation: A physical estimate uses reasonable assumptions rather than random guessing.

questions.stem: A convenient method for estimating the thickness of one very thin sheet is to:

options.text: measure the thickness of many sheets together and divide by their number
multiply the thickness of many sheets by their number

questions.explanation: Combining many thin sheets makes the total thickness easier to determine and then divide.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most important when judging whether an estimate is acceptable?

options.text: It is always greater than the actual value.

questions.explanation: A useful estimate must have a physically reasonable magnitude.

questions.stem: The SI unit watt is associated with:
questions.explanation: Watt is the SI unit of power.

questions.stem: Pressure is defined as force per unit:
questions.explanation: Pressure is force divided by area.

questions.stem: According to the principle of homogeneity, a physically meaningful equation must have:

options.text: equal numerical values on both sides
equal numbers of variables on both sides

questions.explanation: Homogeneity requires identical dimensions on both sides of an equation.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct regarding quantities that are added or subtracted?

options.text: They may have completely different dimensions.
They must have the same dimensions.
They must have the same numerical value.

questions.explanation: Unlike quantities cannot be physically added or subtracted.

questions.stem: Which method should be used first to test the dimensional homogeneity of an equation?

options.text: Compare the numerical values of all variables.
Compare the dimensions of every term.
Draw a graph of all variables.

questions.explanation: Homogeneity is checked by comparing dimensions of every term.

questions.stem: Which statement about a dimensionally homogeneous equation is correct?

options.text: It must always be physically correct.
It can never contain a numerical constant.
Dimensional homogeneity is necessary but does not guarantee complete physical correctness.
It must contain only base quantities.

questions.explanation: Dimensional correctness is necessary but is not proof of complete physical correctness.

questions.stem: Precision of a measurement refers to the:

options.text: closeness of measured value to the true value
closeness of repeated measured values to one another

questions.explanation: Precision means closeness of repeated measured values to one another.

questions.stem: Accuracy of a measurement refers to the:

options.text: closeness of repeated measurements to one another
closeness of measured value to the true or standard value

questions.explanation: Accuracy means closeness of a measured value to the true or standard value.

questions.stem: A set of repeated measurements can be highly precise but inaccurate when the readings are:

options.text: widely scattered around the true value
close to one another but far from the true value
far from one another and far from the true value

questions.explanation: Closely grouped readings can still all be displaced from the true value.

questions.stem: If repeated readings are close to one another and also close to the true value, they are:
questions.explanation: Close grouping indicates precision and closeness to the true value indicates accuracy.

questions.stem: According to the textbook, decreasing the least count of a measuring instrument generally:
questions.explanation: The textbook relates a smaller least count to greater precision.

questions.stem: Uncertainty is best defined as:

options.text: the exact difference between two instruments
the range of possible values within which the true value lies
the average of all measured values

questions.explanation: Uncertainty gives the range within which the true value is expected to lie.

questions.stem: According to the textbook, all measurements contain some uncertainty mainly because of:

options.text: limitations of instruments and experimenter skills

questions.explanation: Practical measurements are limited by instrument resolution and experimental factors.

questions.stem: If two measured quantities are added, their uncertainties are combined by adding their:
questions.explanation: Absolute uncertainties are added when quantities are added.

questions.stem: If two measured quantities are subtracted, their absolute uncertainties are:
questions.explanation: Absolute uncertainties still add even when measured quantities are subtracted.

questions.stem: When two measured quantities are multiplied, their uncertainties are conveniently combined by adding their:
questions.explanation: Fractional or percentage uncertainties are added for products.

questions.stem: When one measured quantity is divided by another, their percentage uncertainties are:
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainties add for division as well as multiplication.

questions.stem: Why can no practical measurement normally be regarded as perfectly exact?

options.text: Physical quantities have no true values.
Measuring instruments have finite resolution and measurements are subject to experimental limitations.

questions.explanation: Practical measurements are limited by instrument resolution and experimental factors.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the role of instrument resolution in uncertainty?

options.text: An instrument can distinguish infinitely small changes.
Every instrument has a finite smallest measurable interval.
Resolution has no relation to measurement.

questions.explanation: Every real measuring instrument has finite resolution or a smallest measurable interval.

questions.stem: Which statement about uncertainty is correct?

options.text: Uncertainty occurs only when an experimenter is careless.
Careful measurement can reduce uncertainty but does not make every measurement infinitely exact.
Uncertainty exists only in derived quantities.
Repeating an experiment makes uncertainty exactly zero.

questions.explanation: Careful technique can reduce uncertainty, but practical measurements still have finite limitations.

questions.stem: Which of the following quantities is dimensionless according to the textbook?
questions.explanation: Strain is a dimensionless variable listed in the textbook.

questions.stem: Which of the following is also dimensionless?
questions.explanation: Coefficient of friction has no dimensions.

questions.stem: A physical quantity that has dimensions but has a constant magnitude is called a:
questions.explanation: A dimensional constant has dimensions but a constant magnitude.

questions.stem: Which of the following is given in the textbook as an example of a dimensional constant?
questions.explanation: Planck’s constant is given as an example of a dimensional constant.

questions.stem: A quantity that has no dimensions but may vary in magnitude is called a:
questions.explanation: A dimensionless variable has variable magnitude but no dimensions.

questions.stem: One limitation of dimensional analysis is that it cannot determine:

options.text: whether both sides have the same dimensions

questions.explanation: Pure numerical dimensionless constants cannot be obtained dimensionally.

questions.stem: Which quantity is associated in the textbook with the precision of a measurement?
questions.explanation: The textbook associates precision with absolute uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which quantity is associated in the textbook with the accuracy of a measurement?
questions.explanation: Smaller fractional or percentage uncertainty corresponds to greater accuracy in this treatment.

questions.stem: A measurement which, on repetition, gives the same or nearly the same result is called a:
questions.explanation: Repeatability of the same or nearly same readings indicates precision.

questions.stem: Which statement can dimensional analysis establish with certainty?

options.text: The numerical coefficient of an equation
Whether an equation is dimensionally homogeneous
Whether every homogeneous equation is physically correct
The value of a dimensionless constant

questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis can test whether all terms have compatible dimensions.

questions.stem: Which statement about uncertainty is correct?

options.text: Uncertainty proves that an experiment is useless.
Uncertainty indicates the possible range containing the true value.
Uncertainty occurs only when an experimenter makes a mistake.
A precise instrument has zero uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Uncertainty expresses the range of possible values containing the true value.

questions.stem: In subtraction of two measured quantities:

options.text: both values and absolute uncertainties subtract
values subtract but absolute uncertainties add
percentage uncertainties must always be subtracted

questions.explanation: Measured values subtract, but their absolute uncertainties are added.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct?

options.text: High accuracy automatically guarantees identical repeated readings.
Precision and accuracy describe different features of measurement.
Accuracy depends only on the number of decimal places written.

questions.explanation: Precision concerns repeatability, while accuracy concerns agreement with the true value.

questions.stem: When two measured lengths are added, the correct uncertainty rule is to:
questions.explanation: Absolute uncertainties are added for addition.

questions.stem: When two measured quantities are multiplied, the correct uncertainty rule is to:
questions.explanation: Percentage or fractional uncertainties are added for multiplication.

questions.stem: A smaller spread in repeated readings would indicate:
questions.explanation: Smaller spread among repeated readings means greater precision.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct regarding repeated measurements?

options.text: Closely grouped readings indicate high precision.
Widely spread readings indicate high precision.
Accuracy can be judged without a standard value.

questions.explanation: Precision is judged by closeness among repeated measurements.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes dimensional analysis?

options.text: It can prove every homogeneous equation is physically correct.
It can determine all numerical constants.
It can test whether dimensions on both sides are consistent.
It can remove uncertainty from measurements.

questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis tests whether an equation is dimensionally consistent.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes Unit 1 measurement philosophy?

options.text: Measurements can have uncertainty and should be interpreted accordingly.

questions.explanation: Unit 1 emphasizes that practical measurements contain uncertainty and must be interpreted accordingly.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes why repeated measurements are useful?

options.text: They allow the spread and average of measurements to be assessed.
They remove the need for measuring instruments.

questions.explanation: Repeated observations allow average values and measurement spread to be evaluated.

questions.stem: A student repeats the measurement of the same quantity under similar conditions and obtains slightly different values. The most appropriate conclusion is that:

options.text: the physical quantity itself must be changing rapidly

questions.explanation: Slight variation in repeated measurements is evidence of measurement uncertainty.

questions.stem: If two students using the same measuring instrument obtain slightly different readings, the difference may arise partly from:

options.text: limitations in experimental skill and reading the instrument
a change in the dimensions of the quantity
the value of a dimensionless constant

questions.explanation: The textbook identifies instrument limitations and experimenter skill as sources contributing to uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which statement best combines the major ideas of Unit 1?

options.text: Physical measurements are exact, dimensions are unnecessary, and uncertainty can be ignored.
Physical quantities can be expressed through units and dimensions, equations can be checked dimensionally, and measurements must be interpreted with precision, accuracy, and uncertainty in mind.
Only base quantities possess units and dimensions.
Dimensional analysis can determine every physical equation exactly.

questions.explanation: It correctly links units, dimensions, dimensional analysis, and measurement uncertainty—the central ideas of Unit 1.
